1 - Introduction
This document is intended for a new employee who will be taking over the Machine Learning Pipeline for Automated Extraction of Articles from Newspaper Archives, a project I developed during my internship at Ouest-France.
As part of my 3rd year academic program at Epitech, i completed this internship to design and implement a custom Machine Learning Pipeline for Automated Extraction of Articles from Newspaper Archives, this pipeline is specifically made for newspaper page from Ouest-France and it’s former name Ouest-Éclair, covering the period from 1899 to 2000.
The archive contains over 10 million pages, many of them are degraded and have complex layouts due to the multicolumn formatting and the inconsistent newspaper typography style that evolved over the century. Ouest-France aimed to develop a solution that not only addressed these technical challenges, but also aligned with its internal AI strategy particularly respecting data sovereignty and ethical AI usage. As a result, all processing had to be done locally, without relying on external tools or cloud based services that could compromise the integrity or ownership of the archives.
Because of these constraints, the entire pipeline had to be built from scratch using open source models and run entirely locally, ensuring that no historical data left the company’s infrastructure.
This report provides a comprehensive overview of the company, the structure of the team I worked with, the architecture of the pipeline, and the challenges faced throughout development. It also includes a detailed breakdown of each component of each step including OCR processing, layout detection, article segmentation, and evaluation methods to ensure you can continue working on the project effectively even after the end of my internship.
By reading this document, you will gain a clear understanding of the technical choices I made and the approaches I explored at each stage of the pipeline. I explain what worked well and what did not, so you can avoid revisiting already tested methods. The reasoning behind each decision is also detailed, allowing you to continue the project confidently.

2.3 - Internal AI Strategy & Data Sovereignty
Ouest-France has established a clear framework for the ethical and responsible use of artificial intelligence, formalized through its internal AI Charter. This charter outlines key principles guiding the integration of AI technologies within the company, ensuring alignment with journalistic values, editorial independence, and data protection standards.
The notion of data sovereignty is really important in Ouest-France, all historical and editorial content need to remain under full control at all times. This means that no external AI providers or cloud services are allowed to access the archives. As a result, any processing involving these documents must be performed entirely locally, using locally hosted models.
Additionally, Ouest-France underlines that AI must serve journalists and enhance their work rather than replace it. The company prioritizes the development and adoption of tools that can help journalists while preserving the human oversight necessary for responsible journalism.
These principles had a direct impact on the design of my project. Through the development of the article extraction pipeline, I made sure to respect data sovereignty by relying only on open source and locally deploy models that I wanted to try.

3 - Project overview
3.1 - Presentation of the Project
During my internship at Ouest-France, my role was to develop an indexing pipeline specifically designed to extract articles from high resolution scans of historical newspaper pages covering the period from 1899 to 2000.
This pipeline was made exclusively for 2 newspapers : Ouest-France and its former title Ouest-Éclair, which changed names after being liberated during World War II (4 August 1944). 
The goal of this pipeline is to index high resolution images of these old newspaper pages, enabling structured access to their content by extracting each article present in them for future research and editorial reuse of historical data, especially for a RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) based on historical newspapers which is a chatbot that is going to use newspaper articles as source to answer question.
There are more than 10 million high resolution archives of newspaper pages that need article extraction in our content bank, the solution needed to be robust, scalable, and accurate, while being fully compliant with our vision for responsible AI and data sovereignty.
3.2 - Key problems addressed 
This project aimed to solve several challenges inherent to the processing of historical newspaper pages from Ouest-France and Ouest-Éclair, covering the period from 1899 to 2000. One of the most significant difficulties was the presence of complex multicolumn layouts, which are common in newspapers but particularly challenging due to the way text blocks, images, advertisements, and tables are tightly packed together.
These layout structures evolved significantly over time varying greatly between decades and sometimes even within the same year depending on editorial choices and special editions, for example at christmas. This variability made it extremely difficult to develop a single, universal approach that could effectively handle all layout variations across such a wide temporal range.
There are also some other problems like the degraded image quality of some pages because when the scan was taken, they set a high contrast to help text extraction. Some pages are also damaged and the text is sometimes faded. These problems complicate text recognition.
In addition to structural complexity, there were also issues related to image quality caused by the contrast. in an effort to improve text visibility during scanning, pages were captured with exaggerated contrast settings. While this helps text readability, images are degraded.
  

Fig. 3.1.1 - Article of Ouest-France from 1975 with degraded image


A major technical constraint came from the high resolution nature of the scans. Pages were stored at resolutions such as 7000x5000 pixels, ensuring clarity when viewed by humans, but posing computational challenges for AI models and OCR tools. Resizing these images to fit standard OCR input sizes caused text to become blurred, so original resolution processing had to be preserved throughout the pipeline.
Furthermore, there was a lack of existing tools specifically designed for this type of task. Traditional OCR engines like Tesseract and EasyOCR performed poorly on these documents due to their inability to accurately interpret old text, inconsistent formatting, and complex layouts. In addition, all processing needed to comply with Ouest-France internal AI vision, particularly regarding data sovereignty.
These combined challenges required the development of a custom built, modular pipeline capable of

4 - Pipeline Architecture
In this section, I will present the overall structure of the indexing pipeline I developed during my internship. Rather than describing only the final system, this section follows a chronological approach,explaining how the pipeline evolved through exploratory research, trial and error, and iterative improvements.
The goal is not only to show what the final architecture looks like, but also to explain how it was built, including the dead ends and unsuccessful approaches that helped to shape the final solution. By detailing what worked and what didn’t, this section aims to provide valuable insight into the development process, so that future work can build efficiently by avoiding an already explored approach that has been proven ineffective and it also underlines the research approach. 
4.1 - Pipeline overview of the indexing pipeline
The indexing pipeline is composed of 3 main stages :
  

Fig. 4.1 - Diagram of the indexing pipeline


As illustrated in Figure 4.1, the pipeline is composed by 3 steps : 
1. Layout Detection :
* Identifies blocks within high resolution newspaper pages, such as text blocks, images, headlines, and advertisements.
* Outputs a list of bounding boxes that define the location of each detected block on the page.
2. Text Extraction (OCR) :
* Converts the detected blocks into text format by extracting the content from the bounding boxes identified during layout detection.
* Outputs a list of text blocks, each containing the extracted text along with its corresponding coordinates.
3. Article Segmentation :
* Groups the extracted text blocks into meaningful articles based on spatial proximity, layout formatting, and contextual information.
* Produces structured outputs representing each individual article, ensuring that the final result is accurate and aligned with the project goals.
Each step builds upon the output of the previous one, ensuring a modular and scalable architecture. This modular design allows for independent evaluation of each component, making it easier to identify bottlenecks or areas for improvement. By splitting the pipeline into distinct stages, we can systematically verify performance at each level, providing a clearer understanding of how the pipeline works and where optimizations might be needed.
Now that the pipeline has been introduced, the following subsections will provide a detailed explanation of each step, presented in the order in which they were explored during my internship. I will begin with Text Extraction (OCR), as this was the first step tackled at the start of my internship. This section will explain my initial approach, what got tested, and the limitations I encountered, which ultimately led me to implement layout detection as a necessary step in the pipeline.
4.2 - Text Extraction (OCR)
One of the first challenges encountered during my internship was being able to extract readable text from high resolution scans of historical newspaper pages. Given that these documents date from 1899 to 2000, some of them suffer from degradation due to age. Additionally, the high resolution of the images, often around 7000x5200 pixels. Is a technical challenge, resizing them for standard OCR tools made the text blurry and unreadable, so the full resolution processing was necessary.
At the beginning of the project, I explored traditional OCR tools that are commonly used in the industry, such as Tesseract and EasyOCR, both of which can run locally on any computer. These tools worked well on modern, clean documents with standard resolution and easy formatting. However, their performance on historical newspapers which feature multiple columns, faded ink, inconsistent fonts, and degraded paper quality wasn’t satisfactory.
Given the complexity of the documents and the need for high quality output, I decided to explore more advanced solutions that might offer better accuracy, even if they required more computational resources. After researching the state of the art in OCR technology, I discovered that the latest approaches leverage Vision Language Models (VLMs), essentially large language models (LLM) enhanced with vision capabilities. These models are particularly effective at understanding document structure and reconstructing damaged or incomplete text, making them ideal for working with historical documents.
The complexity of the newspaper layouts and the need for high accuracy led me to search for more advanced solutions. I decided to explore Vision Language Models (VLMs), which combine natural language understanding with image analysis capabilities. After some research, I chose to test the model named “Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct”, a powerful open-source VLM capable of interpreting complex visual content and reconstructing damaged or incomplete text.
  

Fig. 4.2 - Performance comparison of OCR models
To deploy the model efficiently, I used vLLM, a fast and scalable library for LLM and VLM inference that is widely used in the company. While this significantly improved the quality of extracted text especially for damaged or sections that are hard to read, it introduced a new issue. The model could not process a full page image since the image is in extreme resolution. When I attempted to load entire newspaper pages into the model, the GPU ran out of VRAM, causing crashes and making the system unusable in its current form.
This limitation pushed me to rethink the pipeline design. Instead of feeding the entire page to the OCR engine at once, I realized I needed a preliminary layout detection step. This would allow me to identify and extract only the relevant text regions, which could then be processed individually by the OCR engine without exceeding memory limits.
In summary, while the use of VLM based

4.3 - Layout Detection
After realizing that using OCR directly on the entire newspaper page wasn’t a viable option, due to the resolution of pages I got, I understood that a layout detection step needed to be integrated into the pipeline.
This stage would allow me to identify every article block present on each page. By isolating these regions, I could extract and process them individually using the VLM-based OCR engine without exceeding VRAM limits. The layout detection also provided some additional structural information that would later be used during article segmentation.
At first, I explored layout detection models available on platforms like Hugging Face, hoping to find an easy solution to implement and adapt to my needs. However, most of these models were trained on high quality modern documents, which did not match the degraded, multicolumn nature of historical newspapers. These models performed poorly on our data, and were missing a large portion of text and image.
Given the complexity of the task of handling multicolumn layouts across a century of newspaper pages, with significant variation between each decade in formatting. I decided to focus on SOTA (state of the art) layout detection models capable of working with complex document structures like newspapers.
I then selected a fine-tuned model, his name is YOLO11-Document-Layout-Analysis, based on the YOLO11 (You only look once) architecture, but it has been adapted using a dataset well known in document layout recognition named DocLayNet. The model was first made for object recognition.


  

Fig. 4.3 - Example of Object Detection with YOLO model
As we said before, the model was trained for a specific task, enabling it to now detect 11 classes (Caption, Footnote, Formula, List-item, Page-footer, Page-header, Picture, Section-header, Table, Text, Title). These classes are going to be useful for example if we want later to modify the ocr process to adapt it depending on the type of the layout for example if we want a transcript of the detected pictures.
This model worked reasonably well, however to avoid losing too many articles blocks, it was necessary to lower the confidence threshold for the bounding boxes detection. It also led to an increase in false positives resulting in a large number of overlapping or duplicated boxes. This made the output noisy and difficult to process efficiently in the next stages of the pipeline.
  
  

Fig. 4.3 - Example of Detected Boxes by the Yolo Document Layout Analysis model
As illustrated in the figure above, the initial output from the YOLO model produced a large number of bounding boxes, many of which were either overlapping, redundant, or falsely detected. Clearly, this level of noise would not be usable in the next stages of the pipeline without further refinement.
To improve the quality of the layout detection, I implemented a set of custom rules aimed at reducing false positives and merging related text blocks into coherent zones. The idea came from a presentation I attended during the first week of my internship, where researchers specializing in historical document analysis discussed combining machine learning with rule-based post-processing to enhance detection accuracy.
Inspired by this approach, I developed a series of logic-based rules focused on the position and size of each bounding box, the proximity between neighboring boxes and their potential collisions or overlaps, which could indicate that they belong to the same article.
These rules were designed to post-process the output from the layout detection model by merging overlapping regions, removing duplicates, and filtering out irrelevant or oversized bounding boxes. After implementation, the results showed significant improvement particularly for reducing noise and producing cleaner, more coherent article blocks.




  
  

Fig. 4.3 - Yolo Document Layout Analysis model with rules to merges blocks together
As shown in the figure above, the layout detection now produced a much more structured and readable output. At first, the system appeared to be working very well and indeed, it performed nearly perfectly on about 20 test pages from the 1970s.
However, I soon realized that this was misleading. While the pipeline worked well only on a decade time range, it had only been tested on documents from a single decade. Since the goal was to build a system capable of processing newspaper pages from 1899 to the 1990s, I needed to evaluate performance across a larger temporal range.
To address this issue, I expanded my testing to include representative samples taken every 5 to 10 years, ensuring a better coverage of the wide variety of typographic styles and formatting changes found through the century.
When I applied the same layout detection method to this wider dataset, several issues became apparent. In some cases, text blocks were merged incorrectly, especially in older pages where layout structures were different or less consistent. In others, certain articles were missed entirely due to variations in font style, spacing, or damage to the original page.
This highlighted a key limitation: while the rule-based post-processing improved results for a specific subset of pages, it was not robust enough to handle the full diversity of the archive. This realization led me to explore alternative models and eventually implement an ensemble approach, combining multiple layout detection methods to achieve better accuracy across decades.

4.3.1 - The Ensemble Approach
After realizing that a single layout detection model even with rule-based post-processing was not sufficient to handle the entire diversity of newspaper pages from 1899 to the 1990s, I began exploring alternative strategies that I already knew from prior work. One approach commonly used in the data science field, and well suited to this kind of challenge.
The principle behind ensembling is simple yet powerful, by combining multiple models with different strengths and weaknesses. We can compensate for individual fragility while leveraging each models unique advantages. This leads to more robust and accurate predictions than what any single model could achieve on its own.
To implement this, I needed a second model that could provide high confidence predictions on layout detection, particularly in complex or degraded areas where the first model struggled. This led me to explore additional tools and ultimately build a hybrid system that combined both models outputs in an effective way.
This led me to adopt PP-DocLayout-L, a document layout detection model developed by PaddleOCR, released on March 21, 2025. It’s the largest version of the model, specifically designed for complex document structures and high-resolution images.
Unlike the YOLO based model I had previously tested which was fast but produced many overlapping or redundant bounding boxes, PP-DocLayout-L generated fewer boxes but more confident detections, especially in dense or damaged regions. However, the model occasionally misses smaller or less structured blocks.
To make the most of both models, I implemented a hybrid system that works as follows : 
Since PP-DocLayout-L tends to produce high-confidence predictions, I decided to treat its output as the primary layout detection source. In other words, when it detects a block, I consider it to be more likely accurate compared to the YOLO-based model.
Therefore, the process begins by applying the bounding boxes detected by PP-DocLayout-L. These provide a clean and reliable base structure for most pages, especially those that are degraded or have extremely complex layouts.
Next, I used the output from the YOLO-based model, but this time without applying the stricter filtering rules that were previously used to reduce noise. Instead, these less-filtered results were used to fill gaps where PP-DocLayout-L missed the little zone of the document.
The idea was simple, we start by using the most reliable detections from PP-DocLayout-L, then we use YOLO to find extra blocks that might have been missed. Finally we combine both sets of results and clean them up with some final merging rules that allow us to extend some of the original boxes. This way, I could get the best of both models. At the same time we have the high confidence and accuracy from PP-DocLayout-L and the capacity of YOLO to be sensitive to smaller or irregular blocks from pages

4.4 - Article Segmentation :
The final stage of the indexing pipeline was article segmentation, which aimed to group detected text blocks into meaningful articles. While this part of the pipeline was not fully completed during my internship, I explored several promising strategies that laid the groundwork for future improvements. These explorations were crucial in understanding the challenges and identifying areas for refinement.
The final stage of the indexing pipeline is article segmentation, which aims to group the previously detected text blocks into full articles. This task proved to be one of the most complex parts of the pipeline due to the diversity of newspaper layouts, varying content types and the lack of clear semantic or structural patterns across decades.
At the time of writing, article segmentation remained under exploration, and no fully reliable solution had been finalized. However, I tested several promising strategies that can serve as a foundation for future development
4.4.1 - Embedding-Based Clustering
My first approach involved using semantic embeddings to represent each text block as a vector capturing its meaning. Using these vectors, I built a similarity matrix to identify blocks with related content, hoping to use clustering algorithms to group them accordingly.
  

Fig. 4.4.1 - Embedding Cosine Similarity Matrix 
As we see in the Similarity matrix, there are too few instances of high similarity between the sentences. I then applied HDBSCAN, a density-based clustering algorithm, to automatically detect clusters of semantically similar blocks. However, results were inconsistent :
* Many blocks contained short or fragmented text, making it difficult to extract meaningful themes.
* There was little correlation between neighboring blocks based on semantics alone.
* The model struggled to differentiate articles in the page, and wasn’t able to order blocks that composed articles
This experiment showed that purely semantic approaches are not sufficient for this task without additional contextual or spatial information.
4.4.2 - LLM-Based Grouping Strategy
Given the limitations of the embedding-based method, I explored an alternative using Large Language Models (LLMs). The idea was to pass both the text content and bounding box coordinates of each block to the LLM, asking it to predict which blocks should be grouped together.
This approach also faced challenges:
* Input size became too large when combining many blocks, leading to higher GPU requirements.
* Spatial relationships were not clearly interpreted by the model, even after normalizing coordinate values.
* I attempted to improve performance by pre-extracting article titles using a Vision-Language Model (VLM). Titles are usually larger and easier to detect, so identifying them could help guide the grouping process. However, the title detection step didn’t produce higher quality

4.4.3 - Key Takeaways for Future Development
Although neither method produce a complete solution, these experiments provided valuable insights:
* Semantic similarity alone is not enough, newspaper pages contain diverse content types, and relying only on meaning doesn't lead to coherent grouping.
* Spatial information must be better integrated, layout and position play a crucial role in defining what constitutes an article.
* Hybrid methods will likely be necessary, combining semantic, spatial, and layout information to regroup blocks into articles.
Because my internship has not yet concluded, this part of the pipeline will require further research and experimentation. Any future work on this stage should explore more advanced hybrid techniques, including:
* Group Position Embedding (GPE) : A recent technique designed to enhance the layout understanding capabilities of LLMs without requiring architectural changes or additional pre-training.
* LayoutLM : A LLM model developed for document layout analysis, which could provide better structural awareness than general-purpose models.
* Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) : One of the most promising options, where each detected block is represented as a node in a graph, and relationships between nodes are used to reconstruct full articles. This would require training on labeled data, which I am currently building using recent digital newspapers that already exist in structured formats.
This section is intentionally left open to allow the next person working on the project to continue exploring and refining article segmentation strategies. It represents an area of active research, and any progress made here will significantly impact the overall quality and usability of the indexing pipeline.
5 - Conclusion
My internship at Ouest-France provided a unique and challenging opportunity to develop a machine learning pipeline for the automated extraction of articles from historical newspaper archives, spanning from 1899 to 2000. Through this experience, I gained valuable insights into the complexities of working with high-resolution, multicolumn documents featuring diverse layouts and degraded print quality. This project not only deepened my technical expertise in document analysis and machine learning engineering but also reinforced the importance of adaptability and innovation when dealing with real-world, domain-specific challenges.
One of the most critical takeaways was the necessity of designing a modular and flexible system. By treating each stage of the pipeline (layout detection, OCR, and article segmentation) as independent components, enabled me to iteratively test, debug, and refine each part without disrupting the entire workflow. This modular structure was essential for maintaining clarity and efficiency, especially given the long-term archival nature of the dataset and the evolving requirements of accurate text extraction.
I also learned that standard tools are often insufficient for highly specific and performance use cases. Traditional OCR engines like Tesseract or EasyOCR struggled with complex historical layouts, forcing me to explore more advanced methods using Vision Language Models (VLMs) such as Qwen 2.5 VL (7B), deployed locally via vLLM. This shift significantly improved performance, demonstrating the value of cutting-edge AI models tailored to specific tasks. Additionally, an ensemble approach combining YOLO11 and PP-DocLayout-L enhanced the robustness of layout detection across decades of varied newspaper formats.
Despite progress in layout detection and OCR, article segmentation remains a key challenge, highlighting the need for further research and experimentation. My attempts using semantic clustering and LLM-based grouping offered promising directions but did not yet yield reliable results. Future work could benefit from exploring specialized architectures like LayoutLM, Group Position Embedding (GPE), or Graph Neural Networks (GNN), which may better capture spatial relationships and contextual dependencies among extracted elements.
In conclusion, while there is still room for improvement, especially in the area of article segmentation, my work has established a solid foundation for future enhancements. With continued effort and exploration of advanced techniques, Ouest-France can move closer to building a fully functional and scalable indexing system that unlocks the full potential of its rich historical archives.
